It's difficult to give advice like this, because I don't want to stomp out anything unique in your writing that might become something great later on, but I'll just give one example. Mind you, this is a very subjective sort of critique. 

> The character continued to tread down the road, until he came across a bridge. 

Immediately, you give us a character and sense of space. Awesome.

> He could only see because of the frequent lamp posts evenly spread on the path.

A common alternative would be to imply that the reader already knows we're viewing this scene from your protagonist's perspective. This makes "He could only see" a bit redundant, unless there is something specifically unique about your character's sense of sight.

Often times once the reader is in your protagonist's point of view, you can just go on with descriptions and assume your reader will know who it's coming from. If you used, "Lanterns, evenly spaced, were the only road's source of light." We would know the character is seeing this. He's the only character in the scene so far! 

An alternative is to move the pronoun to add superior mental imagery. Here's a couple lines from the intro of a popular fantasy novel:

"The character peeked up over the knotted boards, scanning the empty town. **Blue lines hovered in his vision,** extending from his chest to point at nearby sources of metal, a result of his unique ability."

He doesn't say, "He could see blue lines..." Instead he turns the visuals into the subject. 

I don't think there's anything wrong about pronoun subject use, in fact the author does that exact thing in the first paragraph of another book, but the repetitious use of it can wear your reader out.

The DX 35mm is fantastic. It's like a reliable companion for me. Perfect for some quick draw street photography on a sunny day.

On a typical zoom lens, your "sweet spot" will usually be neither at the widest focal length nor the lowest aperture. It really depends on the individual lens, though. You can take some tests and figure it out.

I usually shoot with a 35mm f/1.8 prime lens, and it's only slightly softer wide-open; the lens is so good that there's not much of a difference. With my zoom lens (17-50; f/2.8), things begin to look really good around f/5.6.

You're right, I'll just have to invest more time into testing these lenses out. I'm saving up for a huge trip next year, which is why selling the wide-angle lens is so tempting. The other lens is also faster, so I might end up using it at night anyways. (If only I had money for that specific wide-angle lens!)

The standard zoom lens is a very good option for its price. I take mostly urban/street photography though, and rarely 'proper' portraits, so I often find myself on the wider end of things. If you shoot with a similar crop sensor camera like me, you could always grab a budget-friendly telephoto lens. It's inexpensive and sharp, and I know a lot of people shoot portraits with longer focal lengths at f/4. I guess it all depends on your needs. I'd go crazy if I had to swap lenses every time I wanted to go wider than 28mm though!
I have a camera model with an articulated screen. Time to take lots of test footage.

And, yeah, usually some area in the middle will look sharpest. A photography expert has a chart here. Ultimately the only way you can know for sure is by testing the lens yourself, since there is always going to be variation.

I was arrested in a Middle Eastern country after someone accused me of insulting the monarch. The accuser was a local individual at a famous archaeological site who ran scams on unsuspecting tourists. Earlier that day, I had intervened in his scheme, preventing a confused traveler from handing over a small amount of local currency.

I returned to my lodging at 9:00 p.m. and found him and his associates waiting outside, smoking a traditional water pipe. We exchanged heated words a few times. I ended up in the custody of the tourist police.

The tourist police held me for 8 hours. They interrogated me slowly in poor English, and at random intervals shouted, "DID YOU INSULT THE KING?!" I insisted that I had not. Then they transferred me to the main police station. I was to remain there for an indefinite period, until the local authority had a chance to meet with me and determine my legal situation. This was likely not favorable, as I had invoked my right to remain silent for much of the time. However, the local government cares little for foreign legal protections.

Fortunately, I was released around 4 in the morning after a senior officer walked in, shrugged, and instructed them to let me go.

The officer who arrested me handed me a half-eaten bunch of grapes and drove me to the center of the quiet town as a dust storm approached.

The story continues from there, and there were many details I omitted. I plan on writing a book about my experiences one day.
